title: Hazel and the House
premise: Wren Yarrow, a property surveyor raised by a grandmother who taught her to count exits and never answer the third knock, is hired to appraise the old Alder House on Fenwick Lane—the same house where her grandmother once worked as a live-in caretaker. As Wren surveys its rooms, she finds her own childhood photographs altered: an extra chair appears in every frame, waiting, and the house begins appraising her back, measuring what she's worth in years, memories, and blood. She learns the founding Harrow family built the house as a vessel that feeds on a chosen resident to keep itself standing, and that her grandmother survived only by passing the debt to Wren. To end it, Wren must complete the founders' interrupted severance ritual—naming the house, un-naming herself—before the winter solstice when the house takes what it has appraised. In the climax she offers the house not her life but her belonging, giving it the family it was starving for; the house releases her, and Wren walks out owning nothing but a found family of neighbors who refuse to let her be invisible again.
about_author: Elodie Eriksen is a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent a decade cataloguing structurally unsound houses before turning to fiction. Her stories explore how places remember the people who tried to leave them.

chapters.title: The Third Knock
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A routine appraisal of Alder House goes wrong when Wren hears three knocks at a doorless entryway and, obeying grandmother's rule, doesn't answer—but the knocking answers her silence by opening the door itself. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism; Wren convinces herself the wind did it.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Measuring each room, Wren finds her tape measure returns different numbers on every pass, and a child's chalk hopscotch grid appears on the attic floor matching one from her own childhood home. Emotional beat: uncanny familiarity; the house seems to know her measurements better than she does.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, flashback woven in. Sorting her late grandmother's effects, Wren finds a caretaker's ledger from Alder House, 1979–1991, with daily entries counting 'what the house took' in pencil. Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion; grandma knew this house intimately.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reviewing old family photographs for the estate file, Wren discovers every image now contains a plain wooden chair positioned just behind her younger self—an empty seat angled toward the camera. Emotional beat: violation; the past itself has been edited to include her.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Watch
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Wren and Marisol Vega, a retired teacher living across the lane. Marisol warns Wren that surveyors don't last long at Alder House—there have been four, and none finished their reports. Emotional beat: first flicker of connection; someone else sees what Wren sees.

chapters.title: Appraisal Reversed
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The house begins evaluating her: doors open to rooms arranged with her belongings, a written valuation appears on the study desk listing her assets as 'twelve good years, one grief, one talent for being overlooked.' Emotional beat: terror of being seen completely; invisibility offered no protection after all.

chapters.title: The Harrow Papers
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Researching county archives, Marisol finds Ezekiel and Ada Harrow founded the house in 1893 as a 'vessel of continuance' after losing five children, and that every caretaker since signed a ledger line reading 'resident, willing.' Emotional beat: horrified clarity; the house has always needed a person.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Noises
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The noises Wren has explained away for twelve years—since the day grandma brought her to visit Alder House—replay all at once through the walls, each sound now wearing its true source: breathing, chewing, a voice practicing her name. Emotional beat: collapse of denial; the explanations were the price of survival, and they're spent.

chapters.title: Resident, Willing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds her grandmother's signature in the Harrow ledger dated the week Wren turned ten, followed by a blank line with Wren's name pre-written above it in fading ink. Emotional beat: betrayal and heartbreak; grandma didn't escape the house, she deferred it onto Wren.

chapters.title: The Room That Grows
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A nursery appears between the second-floor bedrooms that wasn't there yesterday, furnished with Wren's childhood bed and wallpapered in photocopied strips of her family photos. Emotional beat: suffocating intimacy; the house isn't haunting her, it's adopting her.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol admits she was almost a resident in 1988 and survived by refusing to sign, living forty years under the house's patient watch; she gives Wren the founders' ritual notes she stole decades ago. Emotional beat: guilt and solidarity; survival has costs Marisol never stopped paying.

chapters.title: Severance, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Studying the ritual notes, Wren learns the Harrows died mid-ritual on the solstice of 1901, leaving the house half-bound and hungry ever since; completing it requires naming the house truly and surrendering something it values. Emotional beat: grim resolve; there is a door out, but it opens inward.

chapters.title: The House Makes Its Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The house speaks through the ledger, offering Wren everything she's starved for—a home, permanence, a family—in exchange for simply staying past the solstice. Emotional beat: temptation; the cruelest horror is that the offer is sincere.

chapters.title: Counting Exits
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren attempts to walk away, driving two counties over, but every road bends back to Fenwick Lane and her apartment door opens into the Alder House foyer. Emotional beat: claustrophobic despair; you cannot resign from a family.

chapters.title: What the House Took
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol deciphers the ledger's arithmetic: the house consumed four surveyors' unfinished years, and its hunger peaks at the solstice when the binding thins. Emotional beat: urgency sharpening into fear; three days remain.

chapters.title: The Chair Is Occupied
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the solstice eve, the extra chair in every photograph is no longer empty—it holds a figure made of ledger paper and house dust wearing grandma's cardigan, waiting for Wren to sit across from it. Emotional beat: heartbreak weaponized; the house has learned exactly which face to wear.

chapters.title: Naming the House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At midnight Wren begins the ritual, speaking the house's true name recovered from the Harrows' letters—not 'Alder House' but 'Hollow,' the name the dead children called it—and the walls finally answer. Emotional beat: terrible intimacy; naming it makes it real, and real things can grieve.

chapters.title: Un-Naming
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The ritual demands Wren surrender what the house appraised highest: her belonging. She renounces the Yarrow name, the inherited fear, the twelve years of careful invisibility, feeling herself come apart like wet paper. Emotional beat: ego death as liberation; survival was never the same as living.

chapters.title: The Solstice Hour
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. As the house tries to keep her by force—doors becoming mouths, hallways folding—Wren does the unthinkable: instead of fleeing or feeding it, she sits in the extra chair and offers it the found family it starved for, Marisol's hand in hers, the neighbors gathered on the lawn. Emotional beat: defiant compassion; the house wanted to belong, not to feed.

chapters.title: What the House Let Go
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hollow weeps through every pipe and windowpane, then releases its grip: the nursery dissolves, the chairs vanish from the photographs, and the ledger's final line writes itself—'resident, released.' Emotional beat: exhausted tenderness; even monsters can be mourned.

chapters.title: Final Appraisal
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, Wren files the completed survey marking Alder House condemned and schedules its demolition, keeping only the empty chair as evidence. Emotional beat: quiet closure; some survivals require letting the past be torn down.

chapters.title: Belonging, Found
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On Fenwick Lane, Marisol and the neighbors host a solstice dinner of their own, and Wren—nameless by choice, renamed by invitation—takes a chair set out deliberately for her. Emotional beat: warm resolution; the price of survival was everything, and it was worth it.
